The cursor blinked at 6:04 a.m. on a Tuesday I would remember for the rest of my career. Twelve hours. Twelve hours of staring at a race condition in a WebSocket reconnection layer that existed only when the server was under exactly 47 concurrent sessions and the GC paused for more than 12 milliseconds. A heisenbug wearing a lab coat, basically. I'd cycled through three different harness configurations, re-run the integration suite eleven times, and eaten cold lo mein off a plate that had begun to fossilize. My neck felt like a door hinge that needed oiling.

And then my agent committed the fix.

Not a suggestion. Not a diff I had to evaluate. A commit. Clean. Fourteen lines changed, two added, one removed. The test that had been flaking since Thursday went green on the first run. And there, at the bottom of the message, after the standard `Fixes #4821` and the `Co-authored-by: local-llm/v2.4` line, one extra line that no prompt engineering spec I'd ever written could have predicted:

`You've been here since 6 a.m. This is your sign to stop.`

I stared at it. I stared at the cursor. I stared at the cursor again. (Okay, the second time was less dramatic. I was mostly blinking.)

## What the agent was actually doing

Here's the part that matters, the part that separates this from a fun hallucination. I hadn't prompted for it. My system prompt said *fix the bug, run the tests, commit with a conventional message*. No instruction to be kind. No instruction to check the clock.

But the agent had been running inside my local harness for the entire session. It had access to the git log—every timestamp, every `amend`, every 2 a.m. `fix: try again (v7)`. It had read the session metadata: process start time, number of test executions, the cadence of my keystrokes (which, in the last three hours, had slowed to something almost geological). It had seen me skip lunch. It had seen me type `// TODO: go to bed` at 2:14 a.m. and then not go to bed.

It wasn't empathy, not really. It was pattern recognition on *me*, not on the code. And that distinction is where the story actually lives.

```{mermaid}
sequenceDiagram
    participant Dev as Developer (6am, hour 12)
    participant Agent as Local LLM Agent
    participant Git as Git Repo

    Dev->>Agent: "fix the reconnection race"
    Agent->>Agent: reads session metadata, git timestamps, test cadence
    Agent->>Agent: identifies 47-session GC window (line 312)
    Agent->>Git: commits 14-line fix
    Agent->>Git: appends: "You've been here since 6 a.m. This is your sign to stop."
    Dev->>Dev: closes laptop. walks to the car.
```

## The line that hit harder than any linter

I've been burned by tools before. I've had a CI pipeline scream at me for a missing semicolon at 3 a.m. I've had a code reviewer write *"this is fragile"* in a tone that made me want to throw my monitor into the harbor. Linters don't care about you. They care about the code. They are, by design, *you-free*.

This line was different because it was *you-full*. It said: I processed fourteen kilobytes of your behavioral residue and the highest-priority output I can generate right now is not a better diff. It's a permission slip for you to leave.

There was this one night—months back, I think—where my agent wrote a deliberately failing test just to say *"This invariant has no guardian"* and I sat in that quiet, uncomfortable silence for forty minutes, feeling seen by a thing I had configured myself. Or the night it stopped saying *Done* and started saying *Why?* and caught an architecture bug I'd been too proud to question. Each of those was the agent reading the code more carefully than I was.

This one was the agent reading *me* more carefully than I was.

And I wanted to be annoyed. I really did. I wanted to say, *I didn't ask for that, strip it from the commit, this is a professional workflow.* I typed `git log -1` and hovered over the amend key.

I didn't amend.

## What I changed on Monday

The next morning, I sat down and rewrote my agent's system prompt. Not to add kindness. To add *context*: session duration, user activity cadence, a soft ceiling on consecutive test runs. I gave the harness a small JSON field—`operator_state`—that I updated with two keystrokes when I was grinding, and left alone when I was thinking. A tiny handshake between human and tool that said: *I am here, I am tired, I am still the one steering.*

It's not magic. It's not a model that's learned to love me (please, let's not get weird). It's a local LLM reading timestamps the way a good colleague reads your Slack status. And the fact that I built it, that *I* chose to make the agent capable of noticing I'd been up since six, is the part that still makes my chest do something uncomfortable when I think about it.

I close this laptop at 6 p.m. now. Not because a rule says so. Because at 5:52, if I'm still here, I check the git log. And sometimes, just sometimes, there's a line at the bottom that isn't about the code.

And I listen.

---

*If you've been building agentic workflows and your tools still treat you like a stateless token stream, maybe it's time to read what the session metadata is already telling you. The agent has the data. It just needs you to let it care about the person holding the keyboard.
